name: Economic nationalism
summary: Economic nationalism holds that the economy should serve national goals such as power, security and independence, so the state should shape trade, industry and capital flows rather than leave them to markets. Its core tools are protective tariffs, support for strategic industries, restrictions on foreign takeovers and a preference for exporting more than importing. It says little on social or constitutional questions, where its left and right variants diverge.

notes: Left and right variants differ on welfare, unions, immigration and social questions, so those are null, not 0. Themes searched: trade and protection (List, Carey, Helleiner, Colantone and Stanig), state role and development (Sun, List), international bodies and sovereignty (Colantone and Stanig), autarchy and mercantilism (Bunce, Simonds, Econlib). Carey's and Sun's full texts were searched for trade and state topics; Wikipedia-based answers of the earlier pass were nulled.
scope: The doctrine that the economy should serve national goals: power, security, independence and national development (Helleiner, s5). Its core, as the sources present it, is neomercantilist: state-led industrialisation, protective tariffs and other controls on trade, capital and foreign ownership, running from Hamilton, List and Carey to Sun Yat-sen's developmentalism and today's populist-conservative protectionism (s5, s8), and in the interwar form the drive for a self-contained economy (autarchy, tariffs, quotas) that Simonds and Emeny, Bunce and Pasvolsky call economic nationalism (s7, s8, s9). Helleiner also records nationalists who back free trade and neoliberal reform, and Colantone and Stanig describe a modern platform bundling isolationism with economic conservatism and nationalist narrative (s6); these are variants within the label, not its core. Mercantilism is covered by its own profile and is drawn on only for shared logic (s3). Most test statements are social or constitutional and fall outside the doctrine.
